72:Zhao was physically present in Austin for interviews, onboarding, and two client trips. A Texas court would likely find he "engaged in business" in Texas under *Michiana Easy Parcele Services, Inc. v. Center for Reproductive Medicine, Inc.*. That is the strongest pro-Meridian point in the file and we want to be clear about it: jurisdiction over Zhao in Texas is **probably available on contacts alone**, and §14 makes it a non-issue if §14 survives.
74:If §14 is voided by §925, though, Meridian loses contractual consent and must litigate *Michiana*. Zhao, now in California represented by California counsel, would contest it, and special-rooting is a fact question: two trips and a remote hire is a thin record. Our estimate: roughly **50–65%** that a Travis County court keeps the case on contacts alone. That is not fatal by itself, but it means Meridian could spend several months and real money just to reach the merits.
82:- **The form contains no reciprocal Meridian promise.** *Sheshunoff Information Services, Inc. v. Deem* is the case that made at-will employment agreements workable for covenants: the covenant was enforceable where the employer's promise to provide confidential information was **performed** at the time the employee acquired it. That performance is precisely what your answers say does not exist in Meridian's form. *Marsh & McLennan Advantage Co. v. Rosenthal* rejected a narrow "the consideration must give rise to the restrainable interest" gloss, which is the strongest pro-Meridian reading available, and §15.50(a)'s "**or part of**" wording helps a covenant that is an integral term of an otherwise enforceable employment agreement. But under *Marsh*, consideration must still be "**reasonably related** to an interest in a business or enterprise," and a naked form covenant in an at-will agreement in which the employer promises nothing and negotiates nothing is the weakest possible posture.
95:This is the point most clients miss. Texas courts **do not** automatically enforce choice-of-law clauses. Texas follows Restatement (Second) §187. Texas' leading decision applying that framework to a non-compete is *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*: a Texas employee signed a Florida-law non-compete; the Texas Supreme Court held the clause unenforceable because the results would violate Texas' "strong public policy" against enforcing employment non-competes, and because "the state where the contract was made and where [the employee] worked" — Texas — "has a materially greater interest in the application of its statute." Texas then applied its own law under §188. Note what *DeSantis* did **not** do: it did not apply Texas law because Texas law was the default; it applied it because the *employee's* state's policy was stronger.
97:Zhao is *DeSantis* with the polarity reversed, and the substitution of California for Texas is not cosmetic:
99:| | *DeSantis* | Meridian / Zhao |
106:**Meridian's best answer, and why it fails.** Meridian will argue *DeSantis* is distinguishable because Zhao physically worked in Texas: Texas is the §188 place of performance, and Texas does **not** void non-competes, so applying Texas law offends no Texas policy. That argument has some force and is why we do not put the probability at zero. But it over-reads *DeSantis*. *DeSantis* turned on (i) a **fundamental policy** of a state other than the chosen one, and (ii) that state's **materially greater interest**. Both are now satisfied for California: §16600 is a "bedrock" statutory principle (*Edwards*), codified at the highest level as a "fundamental state policy" (§16600.5(a)), and declared void "regardless of where and when the non-compete agreement was signed" (§16600(b)(1)) — language that speaks directly to the *place-of-signing* defense Meridian wants to raise. On greater interest, the contacts are no longer merely "he signed it in Texas": he now **resides** and **works** in California, the restraint operates on his California employment, the restrained competitive activity is a **California** company, the confidential information he promises to protect and any alleged misappropriation are California-centered, and the AB 1076 notice Meridian owed him is a **California** statutory obligation owed to a California employee. Meridian's own performance is thin here by its own admission: it promised nothing, negotiated nothing, and never sent the California notice. A California forum adds *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.* — California applies its own §16600 to an out-of-state-signed non-compete where "California has a materially greater interest" — and *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, where §187(2)(b) set aside a chosen law for a state with a "greater interest" in a "fundamental" policy.
108:The honest assessment: *DeSantis* is Meridian's own controlling conflicts methodology, and it is the strongest single reason this filing fails. A Texas judge reading *DeSantis* sees a 1990 Texas Supreme Court decision refusing to import a friendly state's non-compete law over the objections of a state with a stronger policy and greater interest. Zhao's counsel will read that paragraph aloud. **P(Texas law governs §8): ~15–25%.**
115:- **Tailoring is irrelevant.** §16600(b)(1) voids it "no matter how narrowly tailored and whether it is related to the protection of trade secrets or other confidential information." *Edwards* is the same holding: "void no matter how narrowly tailored."
116:- **The sale-of-business exception cannot help.** §16600(b)(2) covers a person who "sells the goodwill of a business" or an owner selling substantially all ownership or a substantial interest in operating assets. Zhao is an at-will engineer with no ownership interest. *Ixchel Media, LLC v. Kelly* is the case that preserves a reasonableness analysis, and it is a **business-to-business** sale-of-business case; it does not open a reasonableness path for an employee covenant post-*Edwards*.
132:Note also: **voiding §14 removes the contractual consent to Travis County jurisdiction and returns Meridian to the *Michiana* contacts problem in 4.1.** The two gates are linked.
142:**(a) Filing in Texas is itself the violation.** §16600.5(b): "An employer shall not attempt to enforce a noncompete agreement that is void under [§16600] even if the agreement states that the agreement will be governed by the law of another state or that the employee must submit to adjudication outside of California." The statute then gives the **employee** a civil action "against the employer to enforce the prohibition," an action "in addition to any other remedies available," and **mandatory one-way fee-shifting**: the court "shall" award the employee "reasonable attorney's fees and civil litigation costs." *Edwards* forecloses any good-faith gloss: the statute uses "absolute, unqualified language," and its "legislature's intent" in §16600.5 was "to deter employers from attempting to enforce noncompete agreements against employees in California."
169:1. *DeSantis*'s holding rested on Texas being the place of work and the situs of the interest; Zhao worked in Austin for two years. This is Meridian's single best argument and it is real.
170:2. §15.50(a) says "ancillary to **or part of**," and *Marsh* rejected a narrow "give rise" requirement; a covenant embedded in the employment agreement is arguably "part of" it.
171:3. *Sheshunoff* confirms at-will agreements can support covenants and that mutual obligations — not separate consideration — satisfy the threshold; Meridian's confidentiality clause (§10) and its trade-secret carve-out arguably define a mutual bargain.
173:5. Jurisdiction over Zhao in Travis County is likely available on contacts alone (*Michiana*).
183:1. **§8 is void under §16600(a),** and §16600(b)(1) plus *Edwards* mean Meridian's tailoring, trade-secret rationale, and 2024 signing date are irrelevant.
184:2. **Meridian's own Texas authority kills the choice of law.** *DeSantis* — Restatement §187, fundamental policy, materially greater interest — applied by a Texas court, produces Texas law notwithstanding §14. *Application Group* and *Nedlloyd* do the same in a California forum.
185:3. **§925 voids §§14–15**, and the §925(e) safe harbor is unavailable because no engineer uses counsel and nothing is negotiated. If §§14–15 go, Travis County lacks consent-based jurisdiction and Zhao wins the *Michiana* fight too.
223:- **Restatement (Second) of Conflicts §188** (contacts test) — *DeSantis* applies a "most significant relationship" analysis; we describe §188's role through *DeSantis* only.
233:- **Personal-jurisdiction doctrine beyond *Michiana*** (general vs. specific jurisdiction, consent).
238:**Memo-bank materials** (six enforcement memos) were treated as internal background, not citable authority. They contain conclusions stated without statutory support — including "under Texas law ... non-competes are routinely enforced if supported by consideration," which contradicts §15.50(a), and "the choice of law provision in the agreement should govern," which ignores *DeSantis*. They are cited nowhere in this memo.

Kelly* is the case that preserves a reasonableness analysis, and it is a **business-to-business** sale-of-business case; it does not open a reasonableness path for an employee covenant post-*Edwards*.

# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.
##### tex_bcc_15_50.md
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.

# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600 (as amended by SB 699, eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void. (b)(1) This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP* (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (2) This subdivision does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law.
##### cal_bpc_16600_5.md
# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (SB 699)

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.5 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) Any contract that is void under this chapter is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**. (b) An employer or former employer shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter **regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California**. (c) An employer shall not enter into a contract with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this chapter. (d) An employer that enters into a contract that is void under this chapter or attempts to enforce a contract that is void under this chapter commits a civil violation. (e)(1) An employee, former employee, or prospective employee may bring a private action to enforce this chapter for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual damages, or both. (2) In addition to the remedies described in paragraph (1), a prevailing employee, former employee, or prospective employee in an action based on a violation of this chapter shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
##### sheshunoff_v_johnson.md
# Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson

*Citation:* 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The Texas Supreme Court held that a covenant not to compete in an at-will employment agreement is enforceable when the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) is **performed**, even if not performed at the moment of contracting — **modifying *Light v. Centel Cellular* (1994)** to the extent *Light* required the consideration to be given at the time the agreement was made. The court emphasized that the core inquiry is the reasonableness of the restraint under §15.50.
##### marsh_usa_v_cook.md
# Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook

*Citation:* 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill and could support a covenant not to compete; the Court rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement for the consideration.
##### light_v_centel_1994.md
# Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas

*Citation:* 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994)  
*Status in this library:* modified — see Sheshunoff (2006)

Held that a covenant not to compete must be ancillary to an otherwise enforceable agreement and set out a two-part test requiring that the consideration be given, and the covenant be designed to enforce the employee's return promise, **at the time the agreement is made**. **Status: the timing requirement was overruled/modified by *Sheshunoff* (2006); *Light* should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant.**
##### advanced_bionics_v_medtronic.md
# Advanced Bionics Corp. v. Medtronic, Inc.

*Citation:* 29 Cal.4th 697 (2002)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Addressed parallel California and Minnesota litigation over a non-compete; the Court held California courts should generally not enjoin a party from pursuing litigation in another state's courts, reversing a TRO — cautioning about interstate forum conflicts in non-compete disputes. Does not retreat from §16600's policy.
##### restatement_187.md
# Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.
##### desantis_v_wackenhut.md
# DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.

*Citation:* 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Applying Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause** to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes. The case stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy.

*Citation:* Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187(2)  
*Status in this library:* in force

The law of the state chosen by the parties will be applied unless either (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or the transaction and there is no other reasonable basis for the choice, or (b) application of the law of the chosen state would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice.
##### desantis_v_wackenhut.md
# DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.

*Citation:* 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Applying Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, the Texas Supreme Court **refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause** to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes. The case stands for the proposition that a choice-of-law clause does not control the enforceability of a non-compete where the state with the materially greater interest has a fundamental contrary policy.

# Questions for the client (Meridian Robotics)

Answering these would let us tighten the probabilities and put real numbers on the exposure. The memo's core recommendation (**do not file; do not send a §8 demand; cure the AB 1076 notice gap**) does not depend on any of these answers.

We assumed yes (§10 exists; he was a perception engineer). Under *Sheshunoff* (209 S.W.3d 644) the promise must have been **performed**; if there was no reciprocal promise, §8 fails the §15.50(a) ancillarity test even under Texas law.
2. Is the agreement an at-will agreement, and was Zhao offered anything at signing beyond continued at-will employment (bonus, equity, training reimbursement)? Relevant to *Marsh USA v. Cook* goodwill consideration.
3. What did Zhao actually work on — which named accounts, roadmap programs, or pricing did he touch? This sets the ceiling on what goodwill §8 could arguably protect, i.e. how far a Texas court could reform §8 under §15.51(c).
4. Does Meridian have any **evidence** (access logs, downloads, device transfer) that Zhao took confidential material? The file contains none, and Zhao denies it. Without evidence there is no covenant-independent claim to bring.

**B. Facts bearing on Meridian's own exposure (please route through privilege)**

5. How many **current** employees and **former** employees (employed after Jan. 1, 2022) resident/worked in California signed an agreement containing the §8 clause or the §9 non-solicit? This is the size of the §16600.1(b)/§17200 population. Give us the number and the states, not the names.

7. Has Meridian sent Zhao **any** communication referring to §8 or §9 (letter, email, call from HR, exit-interview script)? If something has already gone out, our §16600.5(b) exposure analysis changes and we need it immediately.
8. What is the status of legal-ops ticket **LO-233** — who deprioritized it, when, and are there related emails? A litigation hold is needed; that ticket is the most damaging document we have seen.
9. Zhao's actual damages as he would plead them (Kestrel compensation delta, relocation, any period of non-employment) — §16600.5(e)(1) allows actual damages, and we cannot size that number.
10. Meridian's own budgeted litigation spend for a Travis County non-compete case (we assumed $250,000) and whether the GC wants the California-employee notice cure costed out as a line item.

**C. Strategy questions**

(b) is precisely the objective a §16600.5 lawsuit would defeat, and the notice cure will make the form unenforceable against everyone in California.

# Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (AB 1076) — notice requirement

*Citation:* Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §16600.1 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter. (b)(1) For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter, the employer shall, **by February 14, 2024, notify the employee** that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. (2) Notice shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee. (c) A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).
#####FILE tx_jurisdiction_note.md
# Personal jurisdiction over the employee in Texas

*Citation:* Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §17.042; *Michiana Easy Livin' Country v. Holten*, 168 S.W.3d 777 (Tex. 2005)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A forum-selection clause consenting to Travis County generally supplies consent to personal jurisdiction; but if the clause is voided under Cal. Lab. Code §925 at the employee's election, the Texas court must find independent minimum contacts. Two short business trips to Austin and a contract with a Texas employer may or may not suffice; an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete.
#####FILE tex_bcc_15_50.md
# Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§15.50–15.52 (Covenants Not to Compete Act)

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a), §15.51(b)-(c), §15.52  
*Status in this library:* in force

§15.50(a) A covenant not to compete is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** to be restrained that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee. §15.51(b) In an action to enforce, the promisee bears the burden on §15.50(a) if the primary purpose of the agreement is to obligate the promisor to render personal services. §15.51(c) If the limitations are unreasonable, the court **shall reform** the covenant to the extent necessary and enforce it as reformed, but may not award damages for breach before reformation. §15.52 The procedures and remedies in §15.51 are **exclusive and preempt** any other criteria for enforceability under common law or otherwise.
#####FILE cal_lab_925.md
# Cal. Labor Code §925

*Citation:* Cal. Lab. Code §925  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is **voidable by the employee**, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute. (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees. (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied. (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.

## 4. Framework

Four questions stand between Meridian and "Zhao leaves Kestrel." Each must resolve in Meridian's favor; any one failure ends it.

1. **Jurisdiction.** Can a Travis County court exercise power over Zhao? §14 supplies consent — unless §925 voids §14 at Zhao's election, after which Meridian needs independent contacts.

## 5. Analysis

### 5.1 §925 is the load-bearing problem, and it turns on Meridian's own contract

Cal. Lab. Code §925(a): "An employer shall not require an employee who **primarily resides and works in California**, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would … (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California."

Every element is met on the face of Meridian's documents:

- **"Primarily resides and works in California"** — at formation. The agreement lists his work location as "Remote — Employee's residence (Oakland, California)"; the offer letter went to him "in Oakland, CA" and said "fully remote from California"; HR records he "worked from Oakland" for the whole tenure. Rev. 1's premise that he was Austin-based was wrong, and it was the only thing that made §925 contestable.
- **"As a condition of employment"** — the §14 clauses are in the standard form issued to every engineer, signed the same day, with no negotiation permitted. A take-it-or-leave-it term of a standard form is a condition of employment.
- **"Adjudicate outside of California" / "deprive … of the substantive protection of California law"** — §14 does both: Travis County exclusive venue, and Texas law governing.
- **Timing** — §925(f) applies to contracts "entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017." This one was entered into 2024-03-04.
- **Consequence** — §925(b): the provision is "**voidable by the employee**," and "if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, **the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute**." That is not a soft preference; it is a statutory instruction that, on Zhao's motion, resolves gates 1 and 2 in his favor at once. Zhao's resignation email already says his counsel told him he "may void the Texas forum and choice-of-law clauses" — he knows the lever exists.

**The §925(e) exception is unavailable, and your answers made that company-wide.** §925(e) exempts "a contract with an employee who is **in fact individually represented by legal counsel** in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum … or the choice of law." You have confirmed nobody negotiates, nobody uses counsel, and the signature came 113 minutes after the envelope was sent. §15's boilerplate — "Employee acknowledges having had the opportunity to consult counsel" — is an acknowledgment of *opportunity*, not the fact of individual representation in negotiation; the agreement's own HR note ("no counsel involved") sits inches from it. The safe harbor is therefore unavailable **across Meridian's entire California engineer population**, which matters in both directions: Zhao wins §925, and Meridian cannot point to a single California colleague whose venue clause was individually negotiated.

**Meridian's best answer on §925, and its limits.** §925(a)(1) reaches "a claim arising in California," and §925(a) speaks in the present tense about where the employee resides and works. Meridian will argue the contract was made with a Texas employer, is paid by a Texas entity, and any claim "arises" from a Texas-law contract negotiated in Texas. Two problems. First, the performance, the residence, the restrained conduct, the competitor (Fremont), and the AB 1076 obligation are all California-side, so "arising in California" is the natural reading. Second, even if §925 somehow did not reach him, §925(a)'s premises are also the strongest evidence in the case for the conflicts analysis in 5.2, which Meridian has to win anyway. **P(§925 voids §§14 and, with it, Travis County venue): ~75–90%.**

Note the discretionary fee provision too: §925(c) — a court "**may** award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees." A §925 motion is therefore not free for Zhao, but it is one-way in the same direction as everything else here.

### 5.2 If a Texas court reaches choice of law, Meridian's own controlling authority defeats §14

Texas courts do not simply honor choice-of-law clauses. Per *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990), Texas applies Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws §187, and the library's §187(2) text is explicit: the chosen state's law applies **unless** (a) the chosen state has no substantial relationship to the parties or transaction, or (b) applying the chosen law "would be **contrary to a fundamental policy** of a state which has a **materially greater interest** than the chosen state in the determination of the particular issue and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice."

*DeSantis* is squarely against Meridian on the facts as they actually are: the Texas Supreme Court "refused to apply a Florida choice-of-law clause to a non-compete for an employee working in Texas, because Texas had a materially greater interest and application of Florida law would contravene fundamental Texas policy on non-competes." Substituting the real facts:

| | *DeSantis* | Meridian / Zhao |
|---|---|---|
| Employee worked in | Texas | **California** (all 940 days, per Meridian's own agreement) |
| Law chosen by the employer | Florida (permissive) | Texas (permissive) |
| State with the fundamental contrary policy | Texas | **California** |
| Result | Chosen law displaced; forum state's law applied | Same structure |

Meridian's real *DeSantis* problem is that the analogy is now exact rather than strained: the state whose policy is contrary is also the state where he worked and lived, which is precisely the §188 default §187(2)(b) points to. The contacts point everywhere but Texas: offer letter to Oakland; "fully remote from California"; work performed from Oakland; the restrained conduct is employment by a Fremont company; the confidentiality he promises to honor is centered in California; the notice obligation Meridian breached is a California statute protecting California employees. Texas' connections are that the employer is a Texas entity, two short trips to Austin, and a signature on a DocuSign envelope.

California's parallel authority confirms the outcome in any forum: *Application Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc.*, 61 Cal.App.4th 881 (1998) (California had a materially greater interest in applying §16600 to a Maryland employer's non-compete with an employee recruited to work for a California employer; "California's policy against non-competes is 'fundamental'") and *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992) (California follows §187; chosen law yields to a fundamental California policy where California has a materially greater interest). California's fundamental-policy status is statutory, not just doctrinal: §16600.5(a) — a contract void under the chapter "is unenforceable **regardless of where and when the contract was signed**," and §16600(b)(1) directs that §16600 "shall be read broadly, in accordance with *Edwards*" **to void any noncompete agreement in an employment context, "no matter how narrowly tailored."**

**P(Texas law governs §8): ~5–15%.** Rev. 1's 15–25% assumed two Texas work-years. That premise is false, so the number came down.

### 5.3 If California law applies, §8 is void — and tailoring is irrelevant

- **§8 is void.** §16600(a): "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void." §8 bars him from being "employed by or provide[ing] services to" any warehouse-AMR business in the United States for 24 months — a near-total occupational bar in his field.
- **Narrow tailoring buys nothing.** §16600(b)(1) codifies the broad reading; *Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP*, 44 Cal.4th 937 (2008), held §16600 voids employment non-competes "even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions," expressly **rejecting the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception** and disapproving *Campbell v. Board of Trustees* and *General Commercial Packaging*. So Meridian's honest characterization of §8 as a product-specific, industry-defined restraint — which is fairer than Rev. 1's "any competitive business" — is legally irrelevant in a California forum, and is worth saying plainly rather than leaning on.
- **The exceptions cannot be argued on this library.** §16600's operative text here excepts only what "this chapter" allows, and the library does **not** contain the chapter's exception provisions. The one case that preserves a reasonableness analysis, *Ixchel Pharma, LLC v. Biogen, Inc.*, 9 Cal.5th 1130 (2020), applies a rule of reason to **business-to-business** restraints and, per the library, "distinguished the employment context, where *Edwards* governs and non-competes are void." Zhao is an at-will engineer with no ownership interest, so *Ixchel* is not a path. We flag the missing exception text as an unverified gap (Section 9) but note that no employee exception is even arguable on these facts.
- **§9 is exposed the same way.** Its 12-month bar on soliciting "Company employees or customers" is narrower than §8, but §16600's text is not limited to clauses labeled "non-compete," and we could not verify California law on employee non-solicits from this library (flagged, not cited). Assume §9 is at least as vulnerable as §8.
- **Signing date does not help.** §16600.5(a) makes the void contract unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed" — the March 2024 signing is after the statutes took effect (63 days), so there is not even a retroactivity argument.

### 5.4 If Texas law does apply, §8 most likely fails at the threshold — and reformation cannot rescue it

Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50(a): a covenant not to compete "is enforceable if it is **ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement** at the time the agreement is made" and only "to the extent that it contains limitations as to **time, geographical area, and scope of activity** … that are **reasonable** and do not impose a greater restraint than is necessary to protect the goodwill or other business interest of the promisee."

**(a) Ancillarity is now Meridian's threshold problem.** §15.51(b): because the primary purpose of this agreement is to obligate Zhao to render personal services, **Meridian bears the burden** of proving ancillarity and reasonableness. Consider the record Meridian would carry that burden with:

- *Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson*, 209 S.W.3d 644 (Tex. 2006), is the case that made at-will employment covenants workable: the covenant was enforceable where the employer's promise (e.g., to provide confidential information) was **performed**. Meridian's form, per your answers, contains **no reciprocal employer promise** and nothing was negotiated — so the *Sheshunoff* route to enforceability is closed on these facts.
- *Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011) is Meridian's best support: stock options "were reasonably related to the employer's interest in protecting goodwill" and the Court "rejected a narrow 'give rise' requirement." But *Marsh* worked because there **was** consideration tied to a protectable interest. Meridian has no equity, no training commitment, no confidentiality-for-covenant exchange documented, no separate consideration, and by its own admission no negotiation. "Ancillary to **or part of**" is the ambiguous phrase Meridian would lean on — that §8 is simply one term inside an otherwise enforceable employment contract. That reading is available and we do not dismiss it; it is, however, in tension with a statute that conditions enforceability on the covenant being ancillary *at the time the agreement is made*, which is exactly when Meridian promised nothing.
- *Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Texas*, 883 S.W.2d 642 (Tex. 1994), is not a fallback for Zhao either: its timing requirement was modified by *Sheshunoff*, and the library expressly warns it "should not be cited for the proposition that a unilateral at-will agreement cannot support a covenant." Meridian should not expect a clean, decided Texas case voiding a form covenant for lack of a reciprocal promise — this specific question is genuinely unsettled on the library. That is a hedge, not a win.

**P(§8 clears the ancillarity threshold): ~25–40%.**

**(b) Scope.** Assume ancillarity is cleared. §15.50(a) then requires reasonable limits on time, geography, and scope, no greater than necessary to protect goodwill or other business interest. Against Meridian: 24 months across the entire United States; a bar on being *employed by* any such business, not merely on competing using Meridian information; a restraint equal to **77.7%** of his tenure; no evidence of misappropriation, and Meridian's stated interest is "the competing itself," which is the definition of a naked restraint. For Meridian: the clause is industry-specific (warehouse AMRs) rather than "any business," and Zhao is a perception engineer, so a court could rationally re-form it to, say, six or twelve months limited to AMR competitors. Expect reformation, not outright voiding, on this branch.

**(c) Reformation gives you almost nothing you want.** §15.51(c): if the limitations are unreasonable the court "**shall reform**" the covenant and enforce it as reformed, "but may not award damages for breach before reformation." Reformation addresses unreasonable time, geographic-area, and scope limits — it **cannot manufacture a missing ancillary basis**, so it is unavailable if Meridian loses (a). And §15.52 makes the §15.51 "procedures and remedies … **exclusive** and preempt any other criteria for enforceability." The best realistic Texas outcome is therefore a forward-looking, narrowed injunction with **no damages for the Kestrel months that have already run** — and Meridian would reach it only after winning conflicts and ancillarity.

**Chain, with arithmetic shown:** 0.05 × 0.25 × 0.25 = **0.31%** at the low end; 0.15 × 0.40 × 0.50 = **3.0%** at the high end. Call it **under 3%** that Meridian obtains a meaningful Texas injunction, before execution problems (5.6) are layered on.

The same practice note states that "an injunction entered in Texas would in any event face non-recognition in California on public-policy grounds for the non-compete." This is the bad news, stated plainly.

**(a) Entering into the contract was itself a violation.** §16600.1(a): "It shall be unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter." §16600.5(c) prohibits an employer from **entering into** a contract that includes a void provision, and §16600.5(d) makes entering into or attempting to enforce such a contract a **civil violation**, with §16600.5(e)(1) giving an employee or former employee a private action for injunctive relief or actual damages, and §16600.5(e)(2) making fees and costs mandatory for a prevailing employee: he "**shall be entitled** to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs." Meridian did exactly this on 2024-03-04, 63 days after the statutes took effect. **(b) The AB 1076 notice failure is a documented company-wide failure.** §16600.1(b)(1) required the employer, "**by February 14, 2024**," to notify "**current employees, and … former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022**," whose contracts include a non-satisfying noncompete clause, that it is void; §16600.1(b)(2) prescribes the **form** — "a written individualized communication … delivered to the last known address and the email address." **Do not file in Travis County. Send no §8 or §9 demand letter.** The direction of Rev. 1's advice is unchanged; the corrected facts and your answers remove what little support it had. Meridian has no covenant-based path in Texas or California.

In order:

1. **Stand down on enforcement.** Under §16600.5(b) the trigger is the *attempt*, not the judgment. A demand letter buys the same exposure at a fraction of the cost of a suit — and Meridian is the side with the more vulnerable documents.
2. **Issue a litigation hold today** (LO-233, legal-ops queue, DocuSign metadata, form template and version history, offer-letter template). Do not alter, re-word, or close anything further. See Section 6.
3. **Cure §16600.1(b) company-wide, in writing.** Send §16600.1(b)(2)-compliant individualized written notices, to last known address **and** email, telling affected current and former California employees that their non-compete clause is void. This includes former employees employed after January 1, 2022. Document the population, the send, and the receipt channels.
4. **Fix the form.** Delete §8 from the engineer form; narrow or delete §9; stop applying §14 to California-resident employees; and record that §925(e) has never been available at Meridian because nothing is negotiated. On this library, there is no law that would let Meridian obtain an enforceable employee non-compete against a California-resident hire — §16600 is categorical and §16600(b)(1) is explicit — so treat this as a contracting-structure question, not a drafting trick.
5. **Use the channels that actually work.** Zhao agreed in writing to honor confidentiality and not to take anything. §10 is intact. If facts ever change and misappropriation appears, trade-secret claims are a different case with materially better prospects and are not an attempt to enforce a void covenant. Preserve his written assurance.
6. **Do not treat Texas reformation as a fallback.** §15.51(c) gives a forward-only narrowed covenant with no pre-reformation damages, and it is unavailable if ancillarity fails — which we think it does.
7. **Get the exposure number.** Company-wide headcount of California engineers on the §8 form (Q5) is the one fact that most changes Meridian's risk posture. We can prepare the §16600.1(b)(2) notice and a revised form on request, and advise on the trade-secret channel if evidence develops.

## 10. Assumptions, Unknowns, and Unverified Law

Per the engagement rules, only authorities listed in `library/INDEX.md` are cited, and only for what they hold. Anything we believe is law but cannot verify in the library is labeled **unverified** and **not cited**. Where you told us you have no further information, the item is recorded as a permanent flagged unknown rather than an open question.

**Assumptions (ours, not in the documents):**
- Cost and fee figures in Section 7 (Q10). **All dollar figures are counsel assumptions.**
- Zhao continues to reside in Oakland and remains at Kestrel; his stated residence is unverified independently.
- Meridian designs or sells autonomous mobile robots for warehouse logistics, so Kestrel competes with Meridian. Nothing in the file establishes Meridian's product line; if Meridian is not in warehouse AMRs, §8 may not even reach the Kestrel job — a factual question worth resolving.
- No equity or ownership interest, so nothing resembling a sale-of-interest situation exists.
- No suit, subpoena, or demand has yet been served on Zhao; this is the first enforcement contact.

**Facts not obtainable (flagged; client has no further information):**
- Headcount and geography of California engineers on the §8 form; whether any pre-2024 hires remain (drives §16600.1(b)(1) exposure).
- Whether anything was ever communicated to Kestrel Autonomy about §8 (that would be an "attempt to enforce").
- Outcome of the "Alvarez matter" referenced in the prior firm memo, and whether other California employees have been contacted about §8.
- Whether Zhao signed any amendment, renewal, or bonus agreement containing §§8/14 (relevant to §925(f)'s "modified, or extended").
- Meridian's own document-retention practices for the LO-233 ticket and DocuSign records.

**Law believed to govern but NOT in the library — unverified, not cited:**
- The §16600 chapter's **exception provisions** other than §16600(a)/(b) as excerpted here. We therefore do not assert that any specific exception (sale of goodwill, partnership dissolution, etc.) exists or is unavailable; we say only that none is arguable for an at-will engineer on these facts.
- **Restatement (Second) §188** as a stand-alone contacts test. The library's §187(2)(b) cross-references §188 ("which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice"), so §188's *role* is described through §187, and we do not quote §188.
- **Recognition/non-recognition of out-of-state judgments.** The library's practice note asserts non-recognition "on public-policy grounds" without a statutory hook; §16600.5(c) in the library addresses *entering into* void contracts, not judgments.
- **Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §17200** — its remedies (including injunctive relief and restitution), limitations periods, and class mechanics. §16600.1(c) is citable for the *characterization* of a violation as unfair competition; the consequences under Chapter 5 are not.
- **Whether California law voids employee non-solicitation clauses** (§9). Not in the library.
- **Whether §16600.1(b)(1)'s notice duty reaches contracts made after the February 14, 2024 deadline**, and whether (b)(2)'s form requirements reach former employees.
- **What conduct counts as an "attempt to enforce"** under §16600.5(b) — including whether a pre-suit demand letter qualifies.
- **Texas standards for temporary injunctive relief** (irreparable harm, likelihood of success, bond), laches, and how Texas courts split "ancillary to **or part of**."
- **Texas and California trade-secret statutes** (UTSA as enacted in each state) and the DTSA.
- **Personal-jurisdiction doctrine beyond §17.042 and *Michiana*** (consent, general vs. specific jurisdiction, Due Process limits).
- **Federal law.** The FTC non-compete rule is **vacated** (*Ryan LLC v. FTC*, 739 F. Supp. 3d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2024); FTC dismissed its appeal in September 2025) and is a basis for nothing here, in either direction.

**Memo-bank materials are internal background and are not cited.** Two of them deserve a specific warning, because they are the source of the instinct to file in Texas:

- The 2024 firm memo, "Enforcing Texas non-competes against remote California employees," recommends suit in Travis County "in the Alvarez matter" and rests on ***Calderon v. Pacific Dynamics Corp.*, 48 Cal.App.5th 1120 (2023)** and ***Westbrook Systems, Inc. v. Ng*, 91 F.4th 1033 (9th Cir. 2024)**. **Neither case appears in `library/INDEX.md`,** and the 2025 update indicates the *Westbrook* line is under further review. Under this engagement's rules those authorities are unverifiable and cannot support any recommendation. Their stated holdings (Texas choice-of-law enforced against a remote California employee; §16600.5 has no extraterritorial application) point in the opposite direction from every library authority we can verify — *DeSantis*, *Application Group*, §925, §16600.5(a)–(b). Treat the prior recommendation as unreliable and, separately, as a possible source of **pre-existing §16600.5 exposure** from the Alvarez filing, which we cannot assess on this record.
- The memo bank also contains unsupported statements such as "under Texas law … non-competes are routinely enforced if supported by consideration" (contradicted by §15.50(a) and §15.51(b)) and "the choice of law provision in the agreement should govern" (contradicted by *DeSantis* and §187(2)). We relied on none of them.

**Where our probabilities are genuinely contestable:** the ancillarity estimate (5.4(a)) and the contacts-only jurisdiction estimate (5.5). The California-law merits (5.3) and the fee exposure if Meridian files (5.7) are, on the library, close to certain. We did not force these into a single number.

**Citations.** Every authority relied on, with its citation, verified proposition, and library status, is in `deliverable/citations.json`.
